question: What is the meaning of adaptability in relation to technical information?
description: The meaning of adaptability in relation to technical information is the ability for users to make additions and modifications to the information as requirements evolve.

the stakeholders and which degree of material reuse is pursued 
(Bouwend Nederland, 2020), the life cycle phase (Wittenveen & Bos, 
2018), the recovery option (Wittenveen & Bos, 2018), and the type of 
materials or components that are used in an object (concrete has 
specifications that require less specific data than a condensing boiler 
(Wittenveen & Bos, 2018)) can differ. Transferability is also a key 
design consideration (Gonçalves et al., 2021) as data needs to remain 
available after systems change, merge, or discontinue (Munaro and 
Tavares, 2021). Especially for long life products, e.g., buildings and 
infrastructure that typically last for 50 to 100 years (Bouwend 
Nederland, 2020), it is difficult to register data in consistent way 
(Chahine, 2021; Munaro et al., 2019; Munaro and Tavares, 2021) as 
it is likely affected by new or changing regulations (B¨ockel et al., 
2020). Translation tables and matching systems could connect 
different classification systems, but usually turn out to be insuffi­
ciently accurate, and time consuming to build (Kovacic et al., 2020). 
Standardized building catalogues (or digital object libraries) are 
adopted more frequently, e.g., Baubook (Honic et al., 2019d; Iaco­
vidou et al., 2018), (NL)/SfB, Uniclass, Masterformat, Omniclass 
(Afsari and Eastman, 2016) openUOB (OpenUOB, 2021) as they may 
help to reduce the number of varieties. What is likely more effective 
is data interoperability, i.e., the ability of systems and services that 
create, exchange and consume data to have clear, shared expecta­
tions (standardized means) for content, context and meaning of data. 
This is addressed in passport projects using linked data (Geonovum, 
2020; Ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en koninkrijksrelaties, 
Kadaster en Stichting FIBREE, 2020; Sauter et al., 2019; Sauter and 
Witjes, 2017). The approach ensures that data is published in an 
explicitly defined way such that it links to other external data sets 
and in turn can be linked from external data sets (Bizer et al., 2011). 
This requires a central registry that issues a Unified Object Identifier 
(UOI) for each main object (e.g, a building or subcomponent), such 
that when objects are linked to data about this object or to compo­
nents it consists of, any stakeholder can always tie this information to 
the object it concerns without the need to register data centrally. 
Several technologies are suggested to broadcast the UOI from the 
psychical product to create the link to a passport, e.g., QR codes 
(Adisorn et al., 2021; Berg et al., 2021; Riedelsheimer et al., 2020; 
Shim et al., 2019), RFID (Berg et al., 2021; Iacovidou et al., 2018; 
Merrild et al., 2016), smart tags (with ink) (Gligoric et al., 2019).
